title: Seller Credits and Concessions: How to Use Them Well
description: Seller credits can cut a buyer's cash to close without a big price change. How concessions work, why program limits matter, and when a credit wins.
image_alt: Two men shaking hands over a model house and keys

faq.a: It's money the seller agrees to contribute toward the buyer's closing costs or prepaid items, shown as a credit on the settlement statement.

faq.q: Are there limits on seller credits?
faq.a: Yes. Each loan program caps seller contributions, and the limits can depend on the down payment and whether the home is a primary residence, second home, or investment.

faq.q: Is a credit better than a price reduction?
faq.a: It depends on the buyer's goal. A credit reduces cash needed at closing, while a price reduction lowers the loan amount and monthly payment.

body_html:
In a balanced or cooling market, seller credits become one of the most useful negotiating tools in a transaction. They can solve a buyer's cash problem, close the gap on inspection repairs, or make a deal pencil without a big headline price cut. But credits come with rules, and getting them wrong can mean money left on the table at closing.

How credits work

A seller credit is a contribution from the seller toward the buyer's closing costs, prepaid items, and sometimes points. It shows up on the settlement statement and reduces the cash the buyer needs to bring. It can't simply be handed over as cash back to the buyer, and it can't exceed the buyer's actual allowable costs.

Program limits matter

Every loan program caps seller contributions. Limits vary by program, by down payment, and by occupancy. Conventional loans tie the cap to the buyer's down payment and occupancy. FHA and VA each have their own limits and definitions of what counts. If the negotiated credit exceeds the cap, the excess typically can't be used and may require restructuring the deal.

The fix is easy: call the loan officer before finalizing the number. We can tell you exactly how much the buyer's specific loan allows and how much of the buyer's actual costs a credit could cover.

Credit vs. price reduction

Seller creditPrice reduction
Buyer's cash to closeGoes downGoes down slightly via lower down payment
Monthly paymentUnchanged unless used to buy down the rateGoes down with a lower loan amount
Seller's headline pricePreservedLower, which affects future comps
AppraisalContract price still needs to appraiseEasier to support

For cash-strapped buyers, a credit often helps more than an equivalent price cut. For buyers focused on the monthly payment, a credit used to buy down the rate may be worth comparing against a price reduction. Run both scenarios.

Common smart uses

  • Covering closing costs for first-time buyers with limited savings
  • Replacing repair requests after inspection, which lets the buyer handle the work their way
  • Buying down the rate to improve affordability
  • Offsetting HOA transfer fees or other costs the buyer didn't expect

Common mistakes

  1. Negotiating a credit larger than the program allows
  2. Negotiating a credit larger than the buyer's actual closing costs
  3. Changing the credit amount days before closing, which can affect the closing timeline
  4. Forgetting that the contract price still has to appraise

Credits after inspection

One of the most common moments to use a credit is after the home inspection. Instead of asking the seller to complete repairs before closing, the buyer requests a credit and handles the work after moving in. That approach has real advantages: the buyer chooses the contractor, controls the quality, and avoids last-minute repair delays.

There are limits, though. Credits can only offset allowable closing costs and prepaids, not pay for repairs directly. If the buyer's closing costs are smaller than the agreed credit, the excess may not be usable. In that case, a price reduction may accomplish the goal better. And if the repair is a health or safety item, some loan programs may require it to be completed before closing regardless of any credit.

Credits used to buy down the rate

A seller credit can sometimes pay for discount points that lower the buyer's rate, either permanently or temporarily through a buydown. For buyers focused on monthly affordability, this can be more impactful than a modest price reduction. Program rules apply, so confirm structure and limits with the loan officer before presenting this option to the seller.

The takeaway

Seller credits are flexible, but they're not unlimited. Confirm the program's cap and the buyer's actual costs before you finalize, and compare a credit against a price reduction based on what your buyer needs most: less cash at closing or a lower monthly payment. A five-minute call with the loan officer makes this easy to get right.
